title: LMML
subtitle: A one-day visit to fifteen London filming locations
author: Claudia Briccolani

cover.intro:
LMML treats London as a museum whose rooms are streets. Its fifteen exhibits are places where a film or a television series was shot between 1964 and 2019: the station where the Beatles run from their fans in A Hard Day's Night, the blue door of Notting Hill, the mews, the chapel and the department store of Love Actually, the market and the bridge of the Harry Potter films, the front door, the park bench and the hospital roof of Sherlock, the café and the restaurant of Fleabag.

This site is the companion to the visit. Each location has its own page, with photographs, a table of data about the place and the scene, and a text; a QR code posted at the location opens the same page on your phone. The map shows every stop, the route of the day and the estimated position and direction of the camera.

Two narratives. The places can be visited in two different orders. Historical timeline follows the release dates of the works, decade by decade, and tells how London on screen has changed; it visits fourteen of the fifteen places. Recreate the shot follows the map, visits all fifteen and is for visitors who want to stand where the camera stood: it adds, at every stop, where to stand, how the light falls and what to look for. Choose one below; you can switch at any time from the menu, and the Previous and Next buttons will follow the narrative you chose.

Texts that adapt to you. On every location page six buttons change the text: Tell me more / Tell me less for the length, Too simple / Too difficult for the level, Do you want to play? / Additional details and references for the tone. A button is disabled when there is no text in that direction. A short French version is available where you see the Français button.

All facts come from the sources cited on each page. Camera positions and bearings are estimated from those sources and have not yet been verified on site; each location page says so.

docs.title: Design choices
docs.text:
The app is a companion for a visitor walking in the street with a phone, so it is designed mobile-first. Content lives in JSON and presentation in CSS: a declarative approach, as the course emphasises active documents over procedural code. The same data must work with any theme and any narrative.

The site is a single HTML page (index.html) that loads one stylesheet for structure (css/base.css), one stylesheet per theme (css/themes/), three JSON data files (data/) and JavaScript ES modules (js/). There is no framework, no build step and no npm dependency. Two libraries are loaded from cdnjs.cloudflare.com: Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map, with OpenStreetMap tiles, and qrcodejs 1.0.0 for the QR codes.

Sections 1.1 to 1.3 describe the canvas, the HTML vocabulary and the layouts of the location page. Section 5 describes how the code is organised.

sections.title: Viewport-sized canvas and scroll containers
sections.text:
It is a requirement of the assignment: “The canvas should be exactly as big as the viewport. Individual texts and metadata viewer will scroll in their own containers within the canvas.” (Course slides, “Warnings”).

The html element has height: 100% and overflow: hidden. The body has height: 100vh, then 100dvh for browsers that support it, and overflow: hidden. The body is a grid whose areas and rows come from two custom properties: --app-areas (default "header" "main" "footer") and --app-rows (default auto minmax(0, 1fr) auto). The main element has min-height: 0 and overflow: hidden.

Scrolling happens only in these containers:

  • elements with the attribute data-scroll (overflow: auto, min-height: 0, overscroll-behavior: contain): the body of every text page (page-body), the text of a location (text-body) and the metadata block (location-meta) in the wide layout;
  • the image strip of a location (location-media), which scrolls sideways with scroll snapping;
  • the opened directions (transition-text), limited to min(40dvh, 16rem);
  • in the narrow layout, the content wrapper of the location page (location-content), which is then the only vertical scroll container of that page;
  • in the wide layout, the location article itself (overflow-y: auto), used only if the rows of a theme do not fit;
  • the site header while the phone menu is open (max-height: 70dvh);
  • the Leaflet map, which pans inside its own box.

For printing, a media query sets height: auto and overflow: visible on html, body, main, the page article and the data-scroll containers, and hides the header, the footer and the print button.

Found with screenshots at 390×844, 844×390 and 1280×800 on 2026-10-06: on phones the location text was not visible at all. The chain from main to the text container already had min-height: 0 at every level; the cause was the grid of the article, whose header row was auto and held the full directions text. An auto row is sized to its content before the flexible rows share what is left, so a long header left nothing for the rows below, and main, with overflow: hidden, clipped them with no way to scroll. The fix bounds every auto row (the directions are closed by default and scroll when open; the toolbar is one row) and gives the article itself overflow-y: auto as a last resort.

Measured before the fix on the location pages, in both themes: at 390×844 the text container had a height of 0 px; at 844×390 it was 47–50 px high and lay entirely below the visible part of main; 44 controls were out of reach and 20 partly cut off. After the fix the same pages show no clipped or unreachable control. The measurements are in screenshots/REPORT.md, which is not part of the published site.

sections.title: HTML vocabulary and style hooks
sections.text:
The assignment says that the HTML vocabulary can, and probably should, be restricted, and to use special classes or data-* attributes. The data-role hooks let each theme restyle and rearrange everything without changing the HTML, which is what makes themes switchable.

The lists below were extracted from index.html, the scripts in js/ and the HTML strings in data/ as they are now.

Elements in index.html (21): a, body, button, div, footer, head, header, html, label, li, link, main, meta, nav, noscript, p, script, select, span, title, ul.

Elements created by the scripts (27): a, article, button, caption, details, div, figcaption, figure, h1, h2, h3, header, iframe, img, li, nav, ol, p, section, span, summary, table, tbody, td, th, tr, ul.

Elements inside the HTML texts of the data files (location texts, transitions, chapter and narrative texts, cover, disclaimer): a, em, h3, li, ol, p, strong. The documentation texts also use table, tbody, tr, th, td, ul, div, figure, img and figcaption.

Classes. The site's own HTML has no class attribute. Classes are used only on the shapes Leaflet draws on the map: lmml-marker, lmml-marker--in-route, lmml-route, lmml-camera-cone, lmml-camera-arrow, lmml-camera and lmml-tooltip. base.css also addresses one Leaflet class, .leaflet-bar a, to enlarge the zoom buttons.

Identifiers. theme-css (the theme stylesheet link), site-menu and site-switchers (referenced by aria-controls of the menu button), and docs-N-N on every documentation section.

sections.title: Portrait and landscape layouts
sections.text:
On a phone the visitor needs, in order, to recognise the place (title, work, picture), to read about it, and to change the text. Directions are needed while walking, not after arriving, so they are collapsed behind a one-line summary. All switches must be visible without scrolling, because changing the text is a core requirement and hidden controls would not be discovered.

The location page has three layouts, selected by media queries in css/base.css. It is wide when the viewport is in landscape, wider than 600px and taller than 500px. Otherwise it is narrow: in portrait, or at most 600px wide, or at most 500px high. A narrow viewport at most 500px high (a phone in landscape) is also short. The section title still says portrait and landscape; these are the conditions actually used.

Wide"header header" / "media text" / "meta text" / "qr text", columns minmax(0, 2fr) minmax(0, 3fr)auto / minmax(calc(var(--loc-image-min) + 3.5rem), 1.4fr) / minmax(0, 1fr) / auto--loc-landscape-areas, -columns, -rows
Narrow"header" / "tabs" / "content" / "toolbar", one columnauto / auto / minmax(0, 1fr) / auto--loc-narrow-areas, -columns, -rows
Short"header header" / "content content" / "tabs toolbar", columns auto minmax(0, 1fr)auto / minmax(0, 1fr) / auto--loc-short-areas, -columns, -rows

The DOM of a location page is the same in the three layouts: an article containing the header, the tabs (Text, Info, QR code), a wrapper (location-content) around the image strip and the three panels (text, metadata, QR code), and a toolbar. In the wide layout the wrapper has display: contents, so the image strip and the panels are grid items of the article; the tabs and the toolbar are not displayed and all panels are visible. In the narrow layout the wrapper is a block with overflow-y: auto and holds the image strip and the one panel selected by the tabs.

In the narrow layout the header shows the title, then one line with the work, the flag 'Not verified' and the directions line. A location that is not a step of the current narrative has one more line: the note 'Not part of “(name of the narrative)”.' and the link 'Return to the narrative', which is 44px high. On such a page the previous / next bar of the shell does not repeat that link in the narrow layout: it shows previous and next only. The chapter line is not displayed in the narrow layout. In the wide layout the header shows the directions line, the chapter line, the title, the work and 'Information not yet verified'; the note reads 'This location is not part of the narrative “…”. It is part of: …' followed by the same link, and the bar of the shell keeps its own 'Return to the narrative'.

The chapter line is hidden on phones for reasons of space; the chapter is introduced by its own chapter screen before its first location.

The toolbar of the narrow layout does not scroll. The six text switches are grouped by axis into three pairs, each under the name of its axis: Length (More, Less), Level (Harder, Simpler), Tone (Play, Details). A fourth group, Language, holds the language buttons. At 390px wide the three pairs fill one row and a second row holds the language buttons and the link 'Show on the map'; in the short layout everything is on one row beside the tabs and the link reads 'Map'. The buttons show their short label in the toolbar and the wording of the assignment in the wide layout. The switch 'Too simple' moves to a higher level and its short label is 'Harder'; 'Too difficult' moves to a lower level and its short label is 'Simpler'. Every switch has the wording of the assignment as its title attribute, and an aria-label made of the short label and the wording, for example 'Harder: Too simple'. Measured at 390×844 in both themes: 9 controls, 2 rows, toolbar 123px high; at 844×390: 1 row, 60px high.

A button label must say what the button does, not how the user feels: “Too simple” asks for a harder text, so it is labelled “Harder”. The full wording of the assignment is kept in the accessible name and in the tooltip.

The text switches and the link to the map are the only elements that change parent. The function placeControls in js/render/location.js appends them to the toolbar when the media query (orientation: portrait), (max-width: 600px), (max-height: 500px) matches, and puts them back (switches first in the text panel, map link last in the QR block) when it does not; it runs when the page is rendered and on every change of that media query, and the listener is removed when the route changes. The same three conditions are written in the narrow layout of css/base.css. The directions to a location are a details element, closed when the page opens at every size. Its summary is built from the transition data: the minutes, then the Underground lines if the transition lists any, otherwise the mode; for example '36 min · Central + Piccadilly lines' or '13 min · Walk'. When opened, the directions are positioned over the page below the header (position: absolute) and scroll in a box limited to min(40dvh, 16rem).

Two sizes are set in css/base.css with a lower limit that a theme cannot go below. Controls: --target-size, default 44px, applied as min-height and min-width max(44px, var(--target-size)) to button, select, summary, the site title, the links of the menu, the previous / next links, the map link, the links of the documentation contents and of the chapter lists, and Leaflet's zoom buttons; the 'Return to the narrative' link of the compact header has the same minimum. Picture: --loc-image-min-height, default 10rem; the value used is --loc-image-min = clamp(6rem, var(--loc-image-min-height), 35vh). It is the minimum height of the picture row of each figure and, plus 3.5rem, the minimum of the media row of the default wide layout. A theme that redefines --loc-landscape-rows replaces that minimum for the media row.

References for the target size: WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA: 'at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels' (W3C, Understanding SC 2.5.5); WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA: 'at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels' (W3C, Understanding SC 2.5.8); Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Accessibility.

The Apple page has a table of control sizes by platform: for iOS and iPadOS the default control size is 44x44 pt and the minimum control size is 28x28 pt (read on 2026-10-11).

The user is outdoors, often walking, using one hand. 24px is the WCAG 2.2 AA minimum (2.5.8); 44px is the WCAG 2.5.5 AAA target and the default control size that Apple gives for iOS and iPadOS.

Measured on the two reference pages after the changes: picture 160–177px high at 1280×800, 160px at 390×844, 104–137px at 844×390; no control smaller than 44×44px at the three sizes in both themes.

docs.title: Metadata model
docs.text:
schema.org is a widely used shared vocabulary that already covers places, films, TV series and images (Uniform, from the RSTU properties in the slides). A separate namespace is used only for facts specific to filming locations that schema.org does not cover, so they are represented as they are, without forcing them into unsuitable terms (Tailored).

The content is in three JSON files. data/locations.json has an @context and a list of 15 locations; data/narratives.json has a list of 2 narratives; data/site.json has the texts of the site, the list of themes and this documentation. The files are plain JSON shaped like JSON-LD: the scripts read them with fetch and do not process the @context.

The @context of locations.json declares "@vocab": "https://schema.org/" and "lmml": "https://claudiabriccolani.github.io/web-tech-proj/ns#". Property names without a prefix are schema.org terms (section 2.1); names with the prefix lmml: are defined by this project (section 2.2). The page at that address, ns/index.html in the repository, lists every lmml: term with its definition; it reads the list from section 2.2 of this documentation when it is opened, and gives each term an identifier equal to its name without the prefix (for example ns#cameraBearing).

Two things were added to each location on 2026-10-13: the official video of its main work, a schema.org VideoObject inside lmml:appearsIn (section 2.1; how the videos were chosen is in section 2.7), and one quiz question, lmml:quiz (section 2.2).

sections.title: schema.org terms
sections.text:
Place rather than TouristAttraction: many locations are ordinary streets, private houses or shops, not attractions.

Movie, TVSeries and TVEpisode: a scene in a series belongs to a specific episode, with the series as its parent.

ImageObject: it carries the author, the licence and the source of an image, which the disclaimer needs.

GeoCoordinates: the place and the camera position each have their own coordinates.

PostalAddress: it holds the street, the postcode and the city of a location, which the metadata table shows on one line as 'Address'.

CreativeWork: each entry of citation is one source, with its address and a one-line description. The metadata table lists the entries as 'Sources' and the disclaimer page builds its list from them.

Person: it holds the name of the director of a film or episode, of the writer of an episode and of the creators of a series, which the metadata table shows as 'Director', 'Writer' and 'Created by'. The author of a photo is also recorded as a Person; the page shows the creditText of the photo.

TVSeason: it holds the season number of an episode, which the metadata table shows as 'Season'.

TVSeries as main work: for 187 North Gower Street and Fleabag's café the data records the series, with its creators and the date of its first broadcast, and no episode. The scene description of the first says that the door is seen in many exterior shots across the series; the facts of the second say that the café was used in the first series and put back to how it was when the second was filmed. The header of the location page and the metadata table then show the title and year of the series.

VideoObject: the official video of the main work. It has name (the title of the video on YouTube), url (its page on YouTube), embedUrl (the address of the player, on youtube-nocookie.com), thumbnailUrl, uploadDate, duration and publisher, an Organization with the name and the address of the channel. It is the value of trailer when the video is a trailer of the work and of video when it is a clip; both are properties of the work, so the video is inside lmml:appearsIn. The location page shows it as one more figure after the pictures: a button 'Watch the video', which the player replaces when it is pressed, so that nothing is requested from YouTube before that. thumbnailUrl is recorded and not shown. The metadata table shows the video under 'Appears in', as 'Trailer' or 'Video clip', and the disclaimer page lists it among the sources.

Question and Answer: the quiz question of a location (lmml:quiz, section 2.2). name is the question, acceptedAnswer is an Answer whose text is the answer, inLanguage is its language and isBasedOn lists the addresses of the sources of the facts it is built from.

Every location is a schema.org Place. The table lists every schema.org term present in data/locations.json, with the number of occurrences in the 15 locations.

sections.title: The lmml: namespace
sections.text:
The definitions of the terms are in the table below. Needs of the project served by the terms: lmml:cameraPosition and lmml:cameraBearing serve recreating the exact shot, which is required by the assignment; lmml:representsPlace serves locations that play other places; lmml:visitorAccess serves planning the visit; lmml:verified, lmml:cameraConfidence and lmml:openQuestions serve honesty about uncertain data.

The other terms: lmml:shotDescription says in words where to stand and where to point the camera, and is shown in the metadata table as 'How to find the shot'. lmml:appearsIn links the place to its main work: the work is named under the title of the location page and on the chapter pages, its details are rows of the metadata table, and its datePublished orders the Historical timeline. lmml:alsoAppearsIn records the other works filmed at the same place, listed in the table as 'Also appears in'. lmml:sceneDescription says what happens in the scene, shown in the table as 'Scene'. lmml:facts holds the statements the texts are written from, each with its source; the data check verifies that every source is in citation. lmml:imageNote tells the visitor, under the images, that no freely licensed photo of the exact place was found. lmml:alt is the alt attribute of each image. lmml:quiz holds one question about the place, in the manner of 'spot the shot', built only from the facts and the shot description of that location; it is shown under the text while the text shown is in the young tone, which is the tone the switch 'Do you want to play?' leads to, and its answer stays closed until the question is pressed. The metadata table does not show it, because the table would give the answer away. lmml:texts, with lmml:length, lmml:level and lmml:tone, holds the texts of a location or of a narrative step and their position in the grid of the assignment, through which the six text switches move. lmml:orderedBy declares the property a narrative is ordered by, so that the data check can verify the order. lmml:estimatedMinutes holds the duration of a narrative; its total is shown on the cover. lmml:transition holds the way from the previous step: its minutes and its mode or lines make the one-line summary of the directions on the location page, and its text is the directions.

sections.title: The text grid (length × level × tone)
sections.text:
The three axes come from the assignment's grid (length / competence / tone). The three cells written for each location cover the extremes and the middle (short · intro · young, medium · average · adult, long · advanced · scholar), so each target audience has a text and every switch has a direction to move in. Short texts also exist in French, for the use case of visitors from Brussels.

Every text has a position on three ordered axes and a language: length (short, medium, long), level (intro, average, advanced), tone (young, adult, scholar), language (inLanguage: en or fr). The grid has 27 cells per language. Only one text may occupy a cell in a language; the data check reports duplicates.

Each of the 15 locations has the same four texts: three in English and one in French. In the narrative Recreate the shot every step also has one English text in the cell medium · average · adult, which replaces the location's text of that cell while that narrative is selected (section 2.5). The Historical timeline has no step texts.

sections.title: Facts, sources and open questions
sections.text:
Every location carries the material its texts are written from. lmml:facts is a list of short statements, each with the address of the source it comes from (169 facts in all). Every such address must also be in the location's citation list (86 entries in all), which feeds the disclaimer page; the data check verifies this, and does the same for the sources of lmml:visitorAccess. lmml:openQuestions records points on which sources disagree or that could not be confirmed.

The metadata table of a location page is generated from the location object. It does not show lmml:facts, lmml:openQuestions and lmml:imageNote (nor identifier, image and lmml:texts, which are shown elsewhere on the page or not at all). It does show lmml:cameraConfidence, as 'Camera data', and lmml:visitorAccess, as 'Visiting and photography' with a source link per statement and the date checked.

Shape of the data. A fact is an object with two properties, text and url. An open question is a plain string, with no source. A citation entry is a CreativeWork with url and description.

In the data now. Each location has between 9 and 16 facts (169 in all), between 1 and 4 open questions (38 in all) and between 3 and 13 citation entries (86 in all). The 86 entries are 63 different addresses, on 19 sites. No fact and no visitor-access statement has a source that is missing from citation. Every location also has 1 or 2 citation entries that none of its facts or visitor-access statements points to.

What the data check does. js/validate.js runs at start-up and writes its findings in the browser console; it never stops the site. For each fact it reports an empty text, a missing url, and a url that is not in the citation list of the same location. For each visitor-access statement it reports a missing url and a url that is not in citation. It does not check lmml:openQuestions, and it does not report a citation entry that no fact uses.

Where the material is used. The disclaimer page builds its list from citation and from the source pages of the images, not from lmml:facts. The metadata table shows citation as 'Sources', one entry per line: the address as a link, followed by the description.

sections.title: Narrative texts and languages
sections.text:
A narrative step may carry its own lmml:texts. Such a text replaces the location's default text of the same cell and language, and only that one; the other texts of the location stay available. The text container records where the shown text comes from (data-text-source: location or narrative).

Texts have an inLanguage. When a location has texts in more than one language, one button per language is shown; the six switches then move among the texts of the current language only. The language chosen is remembered. If the remembered language is not among the languages of the location, the first language of that location's texts is used. All locations currently have English and French, with one French text each, so in French all six switches are disabled.

Step texts in the data now. A step text has the same five properties as a location text: lmml:length, lmml:level, lmml:tone, inLanguage and text. In Recreate the shot all 15 steps have one text each, in English, in the cell medium · average · adult. In the Historical timeline none of the 14 steps has a text.

How the replacement is done. The function mergeTexts in js/textSelector.js builds one list from the texts of the location and those of the step, keyed by cell and language; a step text takes the place of the location text with the same key, and every text in the list is marked with its origin, location or narrative. js/render/location.js calls it with the step of the current narrative. On a location that is not a step of the current narrative there is no step, so only the location's texts are used. The data check looks for two texts in the same cell and language within the texts of one location and within the texts of one step, separately.

Languages in the data now. The 60 location texts are 45 in English and 15 in French; the 15 step texts are all in English. A text without inLanguage is treated as English.

Languages in the code. The languages of a page are those of its valid texts, in order of first appearance. The language buttons are labelled English, Français and Italiano for the codes en, fr and it; any other code is shown as it is. There is no Italian text in the data. The remembered language is the value lang of the saved state, initially en. Pressing a language button saves the language and shows the text of that language closest to the visitor's preference. The text container takes the language of the text shown as its lang attribute.

sections.title: Sources, images and licences
sections.text:
Film stills are copyrighted by the producers, and the site must respect the copyright statement in the disclaimer required by the course. For two places no freely licensed photo exists, and the page says so.

Sources. Each location lists its sources in citation, as CreativeWork objects with url and description. Each fact (lmml:facts) and each visitor-access statement carries the address of one of those sources. The long text of every location ends with a list of references built from the sources of its facts.

Images. There are 27 images, all taken from Wikimedia Commons and stored in img/ as files at most 960px wide. Each has: contentUrl (the file), caption, lmml:alt, creditText (author, licence name, 'via Wikimedia Commons'), creator (the author as a Person), license (the address of the licence) and url (its page on Wikimedia Commons). Licences: 11 × CC BY-SA 2.0, 7 × CC BY-SA 4.0, 3 × CC BY 2.0, 3 × CC BY-SA 3.0, 2 × CC BY 4.0, 1 × CC0. No film still is used.

On the location page. Each image is shown with its alt attribute taken from lmml:alt (the caption is used only if lmml:alt is missing), its caption, and a credit line: 'Credit:' followed by creditText, a link 'License' to the licence and a link 'Source' to the Commons page.

Videos. Each location has one video of its main work, taken from the YouTube channel of the film studio, of the broadcaster or of the band: 11 videos for the 15 locations, searched on YouTube on 2026-10-13. For each video the page of the channel was read on that day, and each was checked to be playable on other sites and available in the United Kingdom and in Italy. The videos were not watched: what each one shows is known only from its title and description.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
The site has two themes, Victorian and Sixties. Each is inspired by one of the works of the tour. Sixties is inspired by A Hard Day's Night (1964), the film of the locations Marylebone Station and Charlotte Mews. Victorian is inspired by Sherlock, the series of the locations 187 North Gower Street, Russell Square and St Bartholomew's Hospital, by way of The Strand Magazine, the magazine in which the Sherlock Holmes short stories were first published in the United Kingdom, from 1891. Each is one stylesheet in css/themes/, scoped with :root[data-theme="…"]. Both were written on 2026-10-11. Neither redefines --target-size or --loc-image-min-height, and css/base.css was not changed for them.

The fonts are not loaded from another site: the files are in fonts/, in WOFF2 format, with the text of their licence (SIL Open Font License 1.1). They were downloaded from Google Fonts, latin subset. Each theme declares its own fonts with @font-face, so only the fonts of the current theme are loaded.

sections.text:
File css/themes/victorian.css. Model: The Strand Magazine, the illustrated monthly in which Sherlock Holmes stories were published with the illustrations of Sidney Paget.

Fonts and colours. Old Standard TT, by Alexey Kryukov, in three files: regular, italic and bold. The body size is 1.0625rem and the line height 1.55. The colours are in the table of section 3. Headings are in the regular weight.

Site header and previous / next. The site title is in italic capitals with wide letter spacing. In the wide layout the header is one row with the menu on the left, the title in the middle and the two switchers on the right; in the narrow layout the title is centred beside the Menu button. A double rule closes the header and another opens the previous / next bar, which stays at the bottom. The position (for example 8 / 19) is in italics.

Text pages. Title centred; the body is one centred column at most 62 characters wide. On the cover the title is inside a double-rule frame, with the subtitle under it in capitals; the two narratives are a one-column list separated by rules, and the current one has a double rule above it.

Location page, wide. Grid areas "header header header" / "text meta qr" / "text media media", columns 2fr 1fr 1fr, rows auto / minmax(7rem, 1fr) / minmax(calc(var(--loc-image-min) + 3.5rem), 1.6fr). The text fills the left half, with a vertical rule on its right; the right half has the metadata table and the QR code side by side and the picture below them. The header is centred. The text is justified with automatic hyphenation; paragraphs have a first-line indent of 1.4em and no space between them.

Location page, narrow. The order of base.css: header, tabs, content, toolbar. The text is not justified; paragraphs keep the indent.

Pictures. Shown in black and white with a CSS filter (grayscale(1) contrast(1.05)); the image files are not changed. Each has a 1px rule around its box and is shown whole (object-fit: contain, as in base.css). The caption is centred, in capitals; the credit line under it keeps its normal case.

Map. The header of the map page is dissolved (display: contents) so that the title is in the first row of the grid, the map in the second and the legend in the third, as a caption in capitals. The map has a 1px border and a 1px outline 3px outside it. The tiles are shown with the filter grayscale(1) sepia(0.25) contrast(0.95). Markers and route are in the text colour and the accent colour.

Controls and details. Buttons have a 3px double border; their labels are in capitals at 0.8em with a letter spacing of 0.08em, because the face has no true small capitals. In the phone toolbar the labels keep their case, because capitals do not fit its columns. The selects have a 1px border in the colour of the text and square corners. The menu, the labels “Theme” and “Narrative” and Previous / Next are in the same spaced capitals, without underline and without a box; the current page is in italic. Previous and Next are at the two ends of their bar, the position in the middle. Level-2 headings of the text pages (for example “Contents”) are centred capitals between two rules. The first paragraph of a location text and of a chapter introduction begins with an initial about three lines high in a double-ruled box, and is not indented. Opened, the directions are in a double-rule frame; their open / closed marker is a triangle drawn in CSS. The keyboard focus is a 1px line 3px outside the control. On the map the zoom buttons are square, with a 1px rule, on the paper colour; the label of a marker has a 1px rule, no shadow, and is in capitals; the attribution is in Old Standard TT on the paper colour.

Reasons, each with the feature of the magazine it comes from:

  • Font: the description of Old Standard TT says that it “reproduces a specific type of Modern (classicist) style of serif typefaces, very commonly used in various editions of the late 19th and early 20th century”. The pages of the magazine that were looked at are set in a serif of this kind.
  • Colours: the pages are black print on off-white paper, and the bound volume of 1894 is blue-green cloth printed in black line. The accent is that blue-green, darkened so that text on it stays readable.
  • Site header: the running head of each page of the magazine (“THE STRAND MAGAZINE.”, or the title of the story) is in centred italic capitals.
  • Previous / next at the bottom: the running head stands alone at the top of the page. This is a layout decision, not a feature copied from the magazine.
  • Cover: the cover of the bound volume has a double-rule border, centred lettering and the line “AN ILLUSTRATED MONTHLY” in capitals at the foot.
  • Location page: page 9 of the July 1892 issue has two equal justified columns with indented paragraphs, and the illustration is set in the lower right with text above it. On phones the text is not justified, because justified lines in a narrow column leave gaps.
  • Pictures: the illustrations of the magazine are black-and-white engravings (those of July 1891 are signed “P. Naumann sc.”), one of them with a ruled border, and the caption on page 9 is in small capitals centred under the picture.
  • Map: it is treated like an illustration of the magazine, framed and with its caption below.
  • Buttons: the cover of the bound volume of 1894 is framed by a double rule, and the panel “Edited by Geo: Newnes” on it has a ruled frame of its own.
  • Menu, switcher labels, Previous / Next: the header of The Graphic of 20 January 1883 has a dateline between rules, with the number at the left, the date in the centre and the price at the right, in capitals and small capitals. The current page is in italic, as the running head of page 9 is.
  • Level-2 headings: on the cover of the bound volume the words “AN·ILLUSTRATED·MONTHLY” are lettered in a break of the rule at the foot.
  • Initial: the illustrated title of November 1891 (page 544) has a capital in a ruled box. That is a title: page 9, in the middle of a story, has no initial.
  • Directions, keyboard focus, map buttons: the double rule of the bound volume, already used for the frame of the map.
  • Labels of the markers on the map: the captions of the illustrations (page 9; Paget’s illustration of December 1892) are in small capitals.
  • The triangle of the directions and the attribution in the face of the theme have no source: the font has no triangle, and Leaflet’s controls were in a system font.

Sources. The Strand Magazine, No. 19, July 1892, pages 9 and 12 (only these two pages were looked at); The Strand Magazine, bound volume of 1894 (the cover of a bound volume, not the paper wrapper of a monthly issue); illustration from the July 1891 issue; Wikipedia, The Strand Magazine (the cover is by George Charles Haité, the Holmes illustrations by Sidney Paget). Font description and licence: the files DESCRIPTION.en_us.html and OFL.txt of oldstandardtt in the google/fonts repository. No source was found on the typefaces the magazine itself used.

Visual references. Six images of British illustrated periodicals of 1883–1894, all in the public domain. The files are copies in img/refs/, reduced to at most 960px wide; they are shown as they are, without the black-and-white filter of the theme.

Other references, as links:

  • Wikipedia: The Strand Magazine (cover by George Charles Haité, illustrations by Sidney Paget)
  • Wikimedia Commons: illustration from The Strand Magazine, July 1891 (engraver's signature, ruled border); public domain

sections.title: Sixties
sections.text:
File css/themes/sixties.css. Models: the grid designed by Romek Marber for the Penguin Crime covers, the UK sleeve of A Hard Day's Night and the magazine Nova.

Fonts and colours. Archivo Black for headings and the site title; Archivo for text and controls (one variable file for weights 400 to 700, one file for the italic). Both are by Omnibus-Type. The line height is 1.5. The colours are in the table of section 3; the red #c8102e is used only for the titles of pages and locations and for the border of the current narrative. Buttons have a 2px black border and bold labels.

The three bands. --app-areas is "header" "footer" "main": the previous / next bar is the second row of the page, under the header. The header is white on black, the previous / next bar is white on the accent blue, and the header of each page has its title in red capitals on white, closed by a 4px black rule. All type is ranged left.

Cover. The body of the cover is a column in which the list of narratives is placed first (order: -1) and the intro after it. The narratives are flat blocks of colour with white text and no border, blue, the current one red, side by side when there is room.

Location page, wide. Grid areas "header header header" / "text text media" / "meta qr media", columns 1fr 17rem 2fr, rows auto / minmax(calc(var(--loc-image-min) + 3.5rem), 2.2fr) / minmax(8.5rem, 1fr). The article has no padding and no gap, so the picture reaches the right and bottom edges of the window; the header, the text, the metadata and the QR code have their own padding and are separated by black rules. The six text switches are set at 0.85em so that they take two rows; their height is not changed. Location titles are red, not in capitals.

Location page, narrow. --loc-narrow-areas is "header" "content" "tabs" "toolbar": the picture comes straight after the header, and the tabs are at the bottom, above the toolbar. The layout for short screens is the one of base.css.

Pictures. In full colour, without border, cropped to fill their box (object-fit: cover). The caption is white on a black band, with the caption text in bold and the credit line in light grey.

Map. Title and legend form a band above the map, closed by the 4px rule; the map reaches the edges of the window, as in base.css. Tiles keep their colours. Markers are red, markers of the current route and camera cones blue, the route black.

Controls and details. The menu is in bold capitals without underline; the current page is a white block with red lettering. The switchers are white on black with a 2px white border, their labels in bold capitals. Menu, Start, Resume, Print, the tabs and Previous / Next have labels in capitals; the six text switches keep their case, for width. Previous and Next have solid triangles drawn in CSS. Level-2 headings of the text pages (for example “Contents”) are white capitals on a black band. The closed directions are a black label with white text and a white triangle; opened, they are a white box with a 4px black border. The keyboard focus is a 3px line in the colour of the text, 2px outside the control, white on the dark bands and blocks. On the map the zoom buttons are square black blocks with white signs in Archivo Black, the label of a marker is white bold capitals on black without shadow, and the attribution is in Archivo on white.

Reasons, each with the feature it comes from:

  • Fonts: “THE BEATLES” on the UK sleeve of A Hard Day's Night is in heavy sans-serif capitals. Archivo is a grotesque sans serif of that kind. It is not a British typeface of the 1960s: its own description calls it “reminiscent of late nineteenth century American typefaces”.
  • Colours: the same sleeve has a blue ground, a title in red on a white band, a black band and black-and-white photographs.
  • Bands at the top, previous / next under the header, type ranged left: on Marber's covers “the title section at the top is divided into three bands”, “with the type ranged left”.
  • Cover: the sleeve is a grid of equal tiles, 20 head shots in 4 rows of 5, under the title bands.
  • Location page, wide: on Marber's covers “the image … occupies just over two-thirds of the space”; here the picture has the largest column. Eye says of Nova that its art directors “offset provocative visuals with unbroken pages of type for reading”, hence one plain column of text beside the picture.
  • Location page, narrow: bands first and the image directly beneath, as on Marber's covers.
  • Pictures: the cover of Nova that was looked at is a photograph that fills the page, with white lettering over it; Eye describes the magazine's “preference for the brutal crop”. The text is placed in a band under the picture, not over it, to stay legible.
  • Map: treated like the pictures, in colour and to the edge.
  • Menu, current page: the sleeve has its title in red on a white band.
  • Switchers, directions, level-2 headings, map buttons and labels: the sleeve has a black band, and in the photograph of Carnaby Street of 1968 the shop sign “John Stephen” is in white capitals on a black board.
  • Narratives as flat blocks of colour: the blue ground of the sleeve, and the shop front “Carnaby Girl” in the photograph of 1968, painted in one red with its name in capitals.
  • Capitals on the controls: “THE BEATLES” on the sleeve and the shop names in the photographs of Carnaby Street are in capitals.
  • Keyboard focus: the hard black rules of 2 and 4px that already separate the bands, after Marber’s banded covers.
  • The triangles have no source: the fonts have no arrow characters.

Sources. Wikipedia, Romek Marber (the quotations on the grid; the page does not name the typeface of the covers); UK sleeve of A Hard Day's Night and a cover of Nova (small reproductions: only what is visible in them is described); “Nova”, Eye no. 10, vol. 3, Autumn 1993 (the quotations on Nova). According to the same article Nova used Windsor wood type; no free equivalent was found, so it is not used. Font descriptions and licences: the files of archivo and archivoblack in the google/fonts repository.

Visual references. The magazines, posters and record sleeves of the 1960s are still in copyright, and no freely licensed reproduction of British printed graphics of that decade was found on Wikimedia Commons (searches of 2026-10-11 for Oz, International Times, Penguin covers of the 1960s, Beatles sleeves and posters, and Swinging London returned no usable file). The three images below are freely licensed photographs taken in Carnaby Street in 1968; they show the lettering and colours of shop fronts and the Union Jacks hung across the street, not printed matter. The files are copies in img/refs/, at most 960px wide.

The printed references of the theme are copyrighted and are given as links only:

  • Wikipedia: UK sleeve of A Hard Day's Night, 1964 (copyrighted; link only)
  • Wikipedia: a cover of the magazine Nova (copyrighted; link only)
  • Wikipedia: Romek Marber (the grid of the Penguin Crime covers)
  • Eye no. 10, vol. 3, Autumn 1993: “Nova” (copyrighted; link only)
  • Wikimedia Commons: “Swinging London”, young adults in Carnaby Street, about 1966; The National Archives UK, no known copyright restrictions (link only)

sections.title: How a theme overrides the layout
sections.text:
What each theme redefines, as the files are now. Victorian: the fonts, the colours, the map colours, --page-max-width, and --loc-landscape-areas, -columns and -rows. Sixties: the fonts, the colours, the map colours, --app-areas and --app-rows, --loc-landscape-areas, -columns and -rows, and --loc-narrow-areas and -rows. Neither redefines the --loc-short-* variables, --target-size or --loc-image-min-height. Sixties adds one variable of its own, --sixties-red.

Three arrangements are made with rules instead of variables, because base.css has no variable for them: the one-row header of Victorian in the wide layout (a grid of three columns); the legend below the map in Victorian (the header of the map page is dissolved with display: contents); the narratives before the intro on the cover of Sixties (order: -1).

Mechanism, as implemented: a theme is a stylesheet in css/themes/ registered in the themes list of data/site.json (id, label, href). js/theme.js sets data-theme on the html element and changes the href of the link with id theme-css, so one theme stylesheet is loaded at a time. Theme rules are scoped with :root[data-theme="id"]. A theme changes the layout by redefining custom properties declared at the top of css/base.css:

  • all custom properties of base.css: --app-areas, --app-rows, --color-accent, --color-accent-contrast, --color-bg, --color-border, --color-fg, --color-muted, --color-surface, --font-body, --font-heading, --font-ui, --gap, --line-height, --loc-image-min, --loc-image-min-height, --loc-landscape-areas, --loc-landscape-columns, --loc-landscape-rows, --loc-narrow-areas, --loc-narrow-columns, --loc-narrow-rows, --loc-short-areas, --loc-short-columns, --loc-short-rows, --map-cone, --map-marker, --map-marker-route, --map-route, --page-max-width, --space-l, --space-m, --space-s, --space-xs, --target-size;
  • --app-areas and --app-rows arrange header, main and footer;
  • --loc-landscape-*, --loc-narrow-* and --loc-short-* arrange the location page (section 1.3);
  • --target-size and --loc-image-min-height can be raised; base.css keeps their lower limits (section 1.3).

docs.title: Narratives
docs.text:
The assignment asks for two or three narratives, with the historical timeline required. The second one serves the use case of Bruno and Beatrix, who recreate shots.

data/narratives.json contains a list of 2 narratives. A narrative has: identifier, name, description (HTML, shown on the cover), lmml:estimatedMinutes, optionally lmml:orderedBy, and chapters. A chapter has: name, text (HTML, shown on the chapter page) and steps. A step has: locationId, lmml:transition (null on the first step of the narrative) and optionally lmml:texts.

The scripts turn a narrative into one sequence of screens: for each chapter, its chapter page, then one screen per step. Previous and next move along that sequence; the address of a chapter page is #/chapter/narrative/number and that of a step is the location page. A location can appear once in a narrative. The current narrative is chosen on the cover or with the switcher in the header, and is remembered.

Arrival times in sections 4.1 and 4.2 are computed from the data for a start at 9:00: the minutes of every transition, plus visitMinutesPerStop at every stop, with no break.

sections.title: Historical timeline
sections.text:

The chapters are decades because the works cluster in distinct periods, from the 1960s to the 2010s, and each decade introduces a different way London was filmed.

The assignment states that “the order (and even the inclusion) of each location in the visit is totally dependent on the narrative proposed to the visitor” (Course slides, LMML project, A.Y. 2025-26, “Narratives”). York Rise was excluded because it was the costliest detour of the route. According to the TfL journey planner, going from St Bartholomew's Hospital to York Rise takes about 41 minutes and from York Rise to Smith & Wollensky about 36 minutes, 77 minutes in all, against about 27 minutes for going directly from St Bartholomew's to Smith & Wollensky: 50 minutes of extra travel, or about 60 minutes counting a 10-minute stop.

The timeline follows the release year of the works, so its route crosses London several times instead of following the map: from Notting Hill to the City, back to Notting Hill and Mayfair, then to the river and up to Bloomsbury. This back-and-forth is intended. The same slide says that visitors “are not simply strolling about the locations in a pseudo-random order, but move back and forward to follow a precise storytelling approach of the app” (Course slides, LMML project, A.Y. 2025-26, “Narratives”). Only locations of the same year are ordered by distance (the two of 1964, the two of 1999, the four of 2003 and the two of 2010), which saves 25 minutes without breaking the chronology.

With 14 locations the timeline takes about 380 minutes of walking and Underground (6 h 20, TfL journey planner) plus 10 minutes at each stop: about 8 h 40 in all.

The minutes are stored in each narrative as lmml:estimatedMinutes.

The route starts in Notting Hill and ends at York Rise, not the other way round, because of one opening time: the Grosvenor Chapel is normally open to visitors Monday to Friday from 8am to 2.30pm (source: the chapel's own site, read on 2026-10-06). Starting at 9:00, this order reaches the chapel at about 11:55; the opposite direction reached it at about 15:30, after closing. The order was computed from TfL journey-planner times between all pairs of locations and is also the shortest found.

sections.title: Text selection algorithm
sections.text:
Only some cells of the grid exist, so a switch moves to the closest existing text in the requested direction, and is disabled when there is none, so that a button never does nothing.

The functions are in js/textSelector.js and use no DOM and no stored state.

Texts considered. The texts of the location and those of the current narrative step are merged: a step text replaces the location text of the same cell and language. Texts with an invalid axis value are ignored. Only the texts in the current language are used; if there is none, all valid texts are used.

Preference. The visitor's preference is one value per axis, stored in the browser, initially medium · average · adult. It is kept from one location to the next.

First text of a page. The text with the smallest distance from the preference, the distance being the sum over the three axes of the difference in rank; ties go to the text nearest the centre of the grid (medium, average, adult).

A switch. Each of the six switches moves one step in one direction on one axis. The candidates are the texts strictly beyond the current one in that direction on that axis. Among them the choice is, in order: the smallest step on that axis; then the smallest distance from the preference on the other two axes; then the nearest to the centre. If there is no candidate the button is disabled. When a switch is used, the preference is updated on that axis only, to the value of the text reached, and in the narrow layout the content area is scrolled to the start of the text.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The site is static and must be published on GitHub Pages without a build step, and every part must be explainable at the exam. The course emphasises combining existing technologies (Leaflet, a QR library) rather than heavy tooling.

How the code is organised. Everything here describes the files as they are in the repository.

sections.title: Start-up and routing
sections.text:
js/app.js is the only script loaded by index.html. It runs, in order: load the three JSON files; check the data; restore the saved state; apply the theme; fill the two switchers and attach the listeners of header and footer; declare the routes and render the current one. If the data cannot be loaded, a message is shown in main.

The part of the address after # selects the view. js/router.js listens to the hashchange event. For each address it finds the matching route, calls the clean-up function returned by the previous view if there is one (the map and the location page return one), empties main, sets data-view on main to the page of the route, and calls the render function of the route; then the position in the narrative is remembered and header and footer are updated. An unknown address shows the 'Page not found' view.

An address #/docs/3.2 opens the documentation scrolled to section 3.2; section numbers are computed from the position of each section in site.json.

sections.title: State
sections.text:
js/state.js keeps the visitor's choices in one object, saved in localStorage under the key lmml-state-v1. Reading and writing localStorage are protected, so the site works without it. Saved values are checked against the themes and narratives that exist now.

There is no automatic update: the code that changes the state also re-renders what depends on it.

sections.title: How themes and narratives are applied
sections.text:
Themes. The themes are listed in site.json (victorian, sixties). When the visitor picks one in the switcher, the state is saved, js/theme.js sets data-theme on the html element and changes the href of the theme stylesheet link, and the current view is rendered again.

Narratives. When the visitor picks a narrative in the switcher, or presses Start or Resume on the cover, the state is saved and the current view is rendered again. The narrative decides: the sequence followed by previous and next; the position shown between them; the transition, the chapter line and the step text of a location page; the route drawn on the map and the numbers of its markers.

Previous, next, return. On a location or chapter that belongs to the current narrative, previous and next follow the sequence; previous of the first screen is the cover. The last screen of a narrative has no next. The pages outside the narratives follow the order of the menu: cover, map, about, documentation, disclaimer, QR codes; the cover has no previous and the QR codes page has no next, and a narrative is started with the Start button of the cover. From the map onwards these pages show 'Return to the narrative' once a narrative screen has been visited; it leads to the last screen visited in the narrative. A location that does not belong to the current narrative is placed after the map: previous shows it on the map, next leads to the about page. A chapter of the other narrative and an unknown address are placed after the cover: previous leads to the cover, next to the map. Both show 'Return to the narrative'. So every page has the pair previous / next, with one of the two disabled only on the four pages named above. The left and right arrow keys follow previous and next.

Map. js/render/map.js draws, for every location, a circle marker at geo, a view cone 45 metres long and 40 degrees wide from lmml:cameraPosition along lmml:cameraBearing, an arrow along the same direction and a dot at the camera position; and one dashed line through the steps of the current narrative in order. A marker opens the location page. #/map/identifier centres the map on one location.

QR codes. Each location page and the QR sheet draw a code that encodes baseUrl of site.json followed by #/location/identifier; if baseUrl is empty the address of the current page is used.

sections.title: Moving the controls into the toolbar on narrow screens
sections.text:
CSS alone cannot move an element out of its parent, and the switches must sit in the bottom toolbar only on narrow screens.

js/render/location.js builds the text switches inside the text panel and the link 'Show on the map' inside the QR block. The article also contains an empty element, location-toolbar. The function placeControls(article, isNarrow) appends the element text-controls and the map link to the toolbar when isNarrow is true; when it is false it puts text-controls back as first child of the text panel and the map link as last child of the QR block. Moving an element keeps its listeners.

renderLocation creates a MediaQueryList with window.matchMedia for the query (orientation: portrait), (max-width: 600px), (max-height: 500px), calls placeControls once and again on every change event of that query, and returns a function that removes the listener; the router calls that function before rendering the next view.

The same query is written in the narrow layout of css/base.css, where the toolbar and the tabs are displayed and laid out. The two must be changed together.

Checked on 2026-10-06 by resizing one page from 390×844 to 1280×800 and to 844×390: the switches and the link were in the toolbar, back in their panels, and in the toolbar again.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Camera positions and bearings are estimated from the cited sources and have not yet been verified on site. Every location has lmml:verified false and lmml:cameraConfidence estimated, and every location page shows 'Information not yet verified'.

Two locations have no freely licensed photo of the exact place: Fleabag's café (20 York Rise) and Smith & Wollensky (The Adelphi). Their pages show the street and the building, with a sentence that says so (section 2.7).

Opening hours were checked on 6 October 2026 on the sites of the venues (Grosvenor Chapel, Selfridges, Tate Modern, Smith & Wollensky) and may change.

Smith & Wollensky and some interiors may require booking: the restaurant takes table bookings on its site, and Tate Modern recommends booking for its exhibitions.

The videos are played from YouTube and were not watched when they were chosen (section 2.7). A channel can withdraw a video or limit the countries where it plays; the page then shows the message of the YouTube player in place of the video.

The quiz questions are in English only: they are also shown, in English, under the French text.
